beats: Hook (slide 8): double the document and attention costs four times as much; at a million tokens one GPU cannot hold it (line_cp_handshake_party for the square law, line_cp_scroll_crush for the size; reuse line_scroll_reader).

Why: attention compute grows with the square of the length, activations with the length, so the sequence itself has to be split across GPUs; the old sequence parallelism still needs the whole sequence per head (slide 9).
The split: cut the long sequence into equal pieces, one per GPU (line_cp_scroll_cut_four, the cover; reuse line_scissors_strips).
The free part (slide 10): projections work token by token, so each GPU works alone on its piece and CP combines cleanly with TP (line_cp_quiet_desks).
The hard part: softmax(QK^T)V needs every token to see every other token, across the pieces (line_cp_peek_over; reuse line_three_readers).

Ulysses (slides 12-13): one all-to-all swap before attention turns "some tokens of all heads" into "all tokens of some heads", and one swap after turns it back (line_ulysses_card_swap, then line_ulysses_suit_piles).
Numbers (slide 14): per-GPU traffic 4Sh/P against 4Sh for TP+SP, constant when length and GPUs grow together; Ulysses passes TP near 32K tokens (slide 15): taped slides and pen work.
Pitfall (slide 15): heads must divide CP x TP; GQA has few KV heads, so they get copied (line_cp_pie_slices, line_cp_photocopier).
Takeaway: TP inside a node, CP across nodes (line_cp_two_houses); next episode: ring attention lifts the head limit.
Cover (line_cover_l07_01; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): four readers each hold up one cut section of the same long scroll, the scissors in a gap.
